Title: Prevent the Deforestation of Rainforests
Brief description: Drawing by Isaac Theo Harris, age 13 (as of 2021) from Budmouth Academy school, Weymouth. Titled Prevent the Deforestation of Rainforests. Coloured ink and graphite on A4 paper, depicting the deforestation of rainforests. This artwork won a Dorset Museum & Art Gallery climate change art competition in 2021.

'On one side of the picture is natures beauty of animals and forests but the other side engulfs and dwarfs it with pollution gasses, whilst cranes and machines cut down the last trees and forest fires rage. The key message is stop chopping down trees and start planting because this will greatly reduce the greenhouse gasses entering the atmosphere.' - Isaac Theo Harris.

title: 250 square kilometres of rainforest burnt today
description:
Poster issued by the Norweigian Conservation Organisation 'Framtiden i Vare hender' (the Future is in our hands) c. 1990
Lettered 'Photo WWF' (World Wide Fund for Nature) and printed with the organisation's logo. 

N.T.B. is the Norweigian Telecommunications Bureau. The poster quotes one of the their announcements. In 'The Greenhouse Effect'  by John Ardill and Stewart Boyle, 1989, the authors advise that the exact figures for rainforest dimensions vary: 110,000 square km per year in the most commonly quoted, but they also advise that 130,000 sq. km may have been lost in the Amazon Basin alone in 1987. A more recent figure issued by the Rainforest Foundation in that worldwide, areas totalling the equivalent of the whole of the USA have already been cleared.

mds.objectHistory:
In 2014, with support from World Wildlife Foundation (WWF) and Sky Rainforest Rescue, actress and former model Lily Cole teamed up with ethical footwear brand Veja to launch a range of trainers made with wild rubber. The trainers’ uppers are made from organic cotton and the soles contain 40 to 50% wild rubber. Inspired by her visits to the rainforest, Cole designed a print for the trainers in three different colourways. 

Rubber trees grow naturally in the Amazon rainforest. The wild rubber trade is managed by skilled local families who extract the sap from the trees without damaging or cutting them down. Environmental campaigners argue that the wild rubber trade is a positive and proactive way to protect areas of rainforest. 

Lily Cole is an outspoken supporter of wild rubber and has discussed the subject in interviews with Vogue, NOWNESS, the Financial Times and several other media outlets. Veja is a fashion brand that seeks sustainable materials such as organic cotton, wild rubber and leather tanned with plant extracts. All of Veja’s trainers include wild rubber.  The brand works directly with co-operatives in Brazil producing sustainably-grown organic cotton and wild rubber.

Sky Rainforest Rescue is a partnership of Sky and WWF that began in 2009 with the aim of saving one billion trees in the Amazon rainforest by 2015.
When the trainers were first released, they were sold through several different retailers including Selfridges and Topshop as well as on Veja’s online store. For every pair sold, £10 went to the WWF and Sky Rainforest Rescue project. Subsequently, the remaining stock of trainers was donated to WWF to be sold on their online store, with the full price of the trainers minus postage costs going straight to WWF.

Text:
Environmentalism

Whether about saving the rainforests or promoting public transport, the themes of decades-old environmentalist posters still resonate today. 

The simple, bold graphic of the orangutan points to text with a clear, direct message, while the catchy slogan ‘Carfree Carefree’ cleverly takes the shape of a bus. Both use graphics that encourage us to look more closely.

Title: Stop the burning
Brief description: Poster
Poster, 'Stop the Burning', designed by Jon Crossland for the Body Shop, UK, 1990
Credit line: Given by The Body Shop plc. Reproduced courtesy of The Body Shop
Text: The Body Shop issued this poster to heighten public awareness of the destruction of the rainforests. They had launched their campaign against the burning of thousands of acres of rainforest each year to create cattle ranches in 1989. This was just one aspect of the work done by The Body Shop with the Amazon Indians. For this poster, the colours red, black and yellow were deliberately chosen because of their effectiveness on political posters.

Brief description:
Shoulder bag from pirarucu fish skin and protective cover by Osklen, 2018

Shoulder bag from pirarucu fish skin by Osklen, 2018

Protective cover by Osklen, 2018
Technique: Pirarucu fish live in the Amazon rainforest and are hunted by local people for their meat. As their skins were often discarded, fashion companies adopted the skins as an alternative to leather. While the pirarucu is a protected species, locals rely on pirarucu fishing as an important source of income. Osklen only use fish from government regulated farms consisting of 2.5 to 5 acres in the state of Rondonia in the Amazon. Compared to cattle farming, pirarucu farming generates lower CO2 and methane emissions, reduces the deforestation of the Amazon rainforest, and farmers achieve 40% more productivity by fishing rather than farming. Pirarucu farms provide employment for local communities and a sustainable source of food, while maintaining fish stocks. The fish do not undergo any genetic modifications or hormone treatments and the skins are dried without chromium.
Text:
Fashioned from Nature

PROTECTED SPECIES

Brazilian fashion brand Osklen specialises in luxury products made from sustainable materials. This combination of ethics and aesthetics, underpinned by art and design, represents a new concept of luxury. The materials they use include pirarucu fish skin. As the pirarucu is a protected species, Osklen only use fish from government-regulated farms which provide employment for local communities and a sustainable source of food, while maintaining fish stocks.

Brief description: Tape measure, tagua nut (vegetable Ivory) with ivory spindle, dome shaped, pierced and carved, rose pink tape marked in inches in ink

The tagua nut, known as vegetable ivory, comes from a South American palm tree, phytelephas, which means "plant elephant". The trees are known as tagua palms or ivory palms because the endosperm of their seeds, when left to dry, resemble elephant ivory and can be carved, polished and coloured. The trees, which can be up to 20 metres tall, grow in Panama, Ecuador, Bolivia, Columbia, north Brazil and Peru.

According to botanist Wayne Armstrong: “The seeds have an outer shell (seed coat) and a large white endosperm. Called "taguas" by local Indians of the Napo River, the endosperm of immature seeds is pulpy and sweet - food for people and animals of the region. Mature, dry seeds are so hard that it requires a hacksaw to cut one in half.”

Tagua nuts have been exported from South America since the 19th century, possibly first used as ballast in ships returning to Europe. They were used for small sewing accessories, snuff boxes, buttons, chess pieces, and handles for walking sticks.
Eventually plastic took over and ended the tagua trade – but now, with the destruction of the rainforests in South America and the hunting of elephants for their ivory tusks, the use of tagua is being promoted again: it can prevent the cutting down of the rainforest for farming by providing a saleable, renewable crop, and it can provide an alternative to ivory.
